Q: Project-level recursive monthly forecasting: even with dynamic anchoring, aggregate portfolio forecast drops unrealistically A:

Use = TiDE  + Pytorch Lightning + Gated mechanism (SwiGLU).

I will give you a blueprint and will try to make you understand the script. Play with it and change it for your Production. If you have any questions regarding Tide and Swiglu just message me or comment. I have tried my best to make others understand !!!

The Fall of XGBoost (Local Modeling)

Stop using XGBoost for the future steps. XGBoost is a "local" model. It only sees one step at a time. If it predicts month 1, it has to feed that guess back into itself to predict month 2. By month 12, the errors compound, and the forecast decays into a flatline.

The TiDE Solution (Global Modeling)

TiDE (Time-series Dense Encoder) is a "global" model. It looks at the entire 24-month past ($L$) and maps it to the 36-month future ($H$) as one single mathematical image.

Because the output layer has exactly $H$ neurons, a single forward pass on the GPU generates month 1 and month 36 at the exact same millisecond. Compounding decay is completely eliminated.

Coherent Forecasting : The model focuses $80\%$ of its energy on project accuracy, but it keeps $20\%$ of its "brain" focused on the total sum.  Remember this  :

loss = (1 - alpha) * loss_indiv + alpha * loss_global

Loss = (0.8) × Individual Error + (0.2) × Portfolio Error

Instead of creating multiple separate neural network layers to calculate different things, we build one massive, double-wide machine. We calculate everything in one forward pass, and then chop the tensor into the pieces we need.

The Transformer Pattern: If we need 3 tools for Attention—Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V)—we don't make 3 layers. We make a triple-wide machine and chop it in three:

# 1. The Machine:

self.qkv_proj = nn.Linear(dim, 3 * dim)

# 2. The Chop (Later in the forward function):

q, k, v = qkv.chunk(3, dim=-1)

Applying this to FiLM: Here, we only need 2 pieces: a Scale ($\gamma$) and a Shift ($\beta$). So, we will build a double-wide machine.

The following method that I will show is Affine Transformation(Feature-wise Linear Modulation) .

Now Horizon simply means:

If you want a clinical trial forecast for the next 36 months, your Horizon is 36.

The future calendar(fut) has a Time Dimension (Horizon = 36), but $\gamma$ and $\beta$ do not.  That’s why we use unsqueeze(1). unsqueeze(1) is technically an expansion in terms of dimensionality (the number of dimensions/axes). We take the raw future calendar (fut) and run it through the affine equation: $y = (1 + \gamma)x + \beta$. If the hospital was enrolling fast,

$\gamma$ is large and positive, scaling up the baseline numbers for all 36 future months simultaneously. Whenever you are handing raw data to PyTorch or getting a final calendar out of PyTorch, the universal shape across the industry is always [Batch, Time, Features].I mean, [Batch, Time, Features] as the universal shipping container. It is how data travels. But, TiDE relies on the B-T-C Flattening Rule: It unpacks that 3D [Batch, Time, Features] container and physically crushes it into a flat 2D sheet: [Batch, Time * Features]. [Batch, Time, Features] is just the delivery box. Once the data arrives inside the TiDE architecture, you have to flatten it entirely (2D) Once the calculation is done, you inflate it back into the 3D shipping container ([Batch, Time, Features]) before sending it back out to the world. Q. A Question must arise Why am I using dim = -1 here ?

Ans: It is an industry standard that when dealing with time or language, the tensor should always flow in the exact order of: Group $\rightarrow$ Time $\rightarrow$ Details.

The structure commonly called [B T C ] = [Batch Size (The Group) , Sequence Length (The Time) ,Feature Width (The Details) ]

If The Input (The 3D Assembled Furniture)  = [128 Hospitals, 36 Months of History, 10 Medical Features]

TiDE Shape: [Batch Size, (Sequence × Features)] (Strictly 2D)

=> [128 Hospitals, 360 Flattened Features]

This 2D flattened state is exactly where our SwiGLU layers live.

And this is exactly why  chunk(2, dim=-1) code is brilliant. It chops the 360 in half flawlessly. Also, At the very end of the network (right before the Dual-Head KillSwitch), the TiDE Decoder takes the final dense mathematical vector and physically "inflates" it back into a 3D shape.

TiDE's architecture = 3D Input $\rightarrow$ Flatten to 2D $\rightarrow$ Process via MLPs $\rightarrow$ Inflate to 3D Output.

Inside the Tide Architecture(Hotel Analogy):

volume_head  = only job is to look at the calendar and estimate customer demand.

He thinks, It is a Sunday. We are going to sell 200 plates today.

activity_head (The Operations Director)  = He thinks “Are we legally and physically able to open the hotel today”?

The activity_head looks at the background reality (the data context):

  • Is the food license expired?

  • Did all the cooks call in sick?

  • Is there a local strike shutting down the streets?

Based on that information, the activity_head calculates a raw survival score.

Let’s say it's a Sunday. But all the cooks are sick.

We will introduce a Sigmoid . The Sigmoid Curve takes that negative score and translates it into a strict probability: 0% chance of opening (or 0.0).

We will introduce a softplus which is a smooth curve (mathematically, it is $f(x) = \ln(1 + e^x)$).

At the end of the day, the business formula multiplies the two managers together:

Data Stream ($x_{data}$)  = The Payload (The "What")  = Based on our previous record, we will prepare 200 plates of Biryani today.

Gate Stream ($x_{gate}$)  = The Valve (The "How Much") = All Chefs are Sick.

No one is coming to the Restaurant. The valve is 0% open. = Restaurant Closed.

$$\text{Output} = x_{data} \odot \text{SiLU}(x_{gate})$$

Probability of Opening (0.0) × Estimated Plates (200) = 0 actual sales.

The Reality: The Gate Stream (The Valve) mathematically choked the Data Stream (The Payload) because the context demanded it.

One more thing :

xdata​ (The Payload): The raw pattern (e.g., "Sunday normally means high traffic").

xgate​ (The Valve): The contextual reality check (e.g., "The weather data indicates a massive storm").

The Only Tiny Technical Difference:

=> Macro Level (The Final Output Head): prob_active(Sigmoid) * expected_volume(Softplus). This happens at the very end of the network. It makes the final business decision (e.g., "The project is dead" or "The restaurant is closed").

=> Micro Level (The SwiGLU Block): x_data * SiLU(x_gate). This is the exact same "Valve × Payload" concept, but it happens millions of times inside the hidden layers to filter out bad logic before it even reaches the end.

Now take a situation :

A train is running 100 km/h for the last 10 hours. Therefore, in 1 hour, it will travel another 100 km.

But what if The bridge ahead is completely destroyed ??

their mathematical jobs are exact opposites.

Here is the pattern recognition shortcut :

  • SwiGLU’s job is to IGNORE a zero.

  • The Dual-Head’s job is to CREATE a zero.

  • We use SwiGLU internally to manage Data Quality (filtering out noisy reporting glitches and holidays), but we use a Dual-Head at the output to enforce Legal Reality (forcing the forecast to exactly zero if the FDA halts the trial).

    Let’s say Atlanta Hospital was doing a fantastic job.

  • January: 5 patients enrolled.

  • February: 5 patients enrolled.

  • March: 5 patients enrolled.

This consistent success is its historical momentum.

Then, in April, the FDA legally shuts the hospital down because of a medical emergency. The bridge is destroyed. Then, what will happen ?

We will create 2 more situations to understand why we need both SwiGlu  + Dual Head.

A patient at a hospital in Atlanta experiences a severe heart complication from the experimental drug.

The Action: The FDA  immediately issues a Clinical Hold (a Protocol Halt). That specific hospital is legally locked down. They are forbidden from enrolling another patient until the investigation is over.

Now the SwiGLu  will say : The Historical Momentum for this Atlanta Hospital is Great.

Hence, SwiGlu will predict 5 patients for next month.

But Dual Head(activity_head and volume_head) sits at the very end of the pipeline. It sees the "Clinical Hold" flag and activity_head instantly outputs a probability of 0.0. It mathematically crushes the SwiGLU forecast, forcing the final output to exactly 0. It ensures AI's mathematical prediction perfectly matches the FDA's legal reality.

It tells the forecasting engine: "The hospital is dead. Stop predicting patients immediately."

When a single neural network splits at the very end to predict two entirely different things simultaneously, it is called a Multi-Head Architecture. The Dual-Head kills the forecast due to a permanent reality.The code return prob_active * expected_volume is formally known as a Multiplicative Gate.

Now what will happen if : Only SwiGLU  and No Dual-Head :

The Christmas Holiday (Temporary Zero) : Works Perfectly. The AI smooths over the holiday and keeps predicting patients.

The FDA Shutdown (Permanent Zero)  : Catastrophic Failure. SwiGLU treats the FDA shutdown like a holiday. It smooths it over and illegally predicts 5 patients for a halted hospital.

Only Dual-Head and No SwiGLU :

The Christmas Holiday (Temporary Zero)  : Catastrophic Failure. The Dual-Head sees the holiday drop to 0, thinks the hospital is dead, and permanently flatlines the forecast.

The FDA Shutdown (Permanent Zero) : Works Perfectly. The Dual-Head forces the halted hospital to output exactly 0.

The unsqueeze(1) Necessity:

The unsqueeze(1) command.You apply it to $\gamma$ and $\beta$. Before: [Batch, Features] . After : unsqueeze(1): [Batch, 1, Features]

We will use static_proj. Whenever you see the word proj or "projection" in a modern AI codebase, 99% of the time, it is just a standard nn.Linear machine acting as the movie projector.

Let’s see why static_proj is useful.

In medical Industry :

If we put :

24 hour history + Trial spending per month = $100,000 + Patients per week = 2

Then AI can predict = Too slow + Trial is Failing + Cash is Burning + Prediction of Massive Delay.

But now If we add static_features:

Disease: Pediatric Rare Bone Cancer

Phase: Phase 3

Then AI will sense the real problem and can predict = Finding children with this specific cancer is incredibly hard + treating them is highly expensive + 2 patients a week is actually a great success rate for this specific category. Prediction of  an early finish.

Enrolling 2 patients per week, This Rare Pediatric Cancer Trial will be treated as

Highly Successful or Highly Efficient. That’s why AI will Predict an Early Finish.

I will also use Dropout :

self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout) :

This acts as a Man who fires random workers from the Job.

Actually Neural Networks are notoriously Lazy. If there are 256, then maybe 20 will try to figure out a shortcut to predict the Future and the other 236 will go to sleep.

Let’s say there are 256 men. Now, dropout = 0.1  means 10%.Then, it means 10% of men will be fired everyday if they don't work properly. I will use RMSNorm (Root Mean Square Normalization) which uses a mathematical shortcut: It assumes the center (the mean) is already zero.It skips the mean calculation entirely and only scales the spread (the variance). In modern SwiGLU + RMSNorm architectures (like LLaMA and Production TiDE), we strictly use bias = False everywhere inside the block.
The Final SwiGLU Equation When you write it all out mathematically, the equation transforms into this: y = RMSNorm(x+Dropout(W2​⋅((Wdata​⋅x)⊙SiLU(Wgate​⋅x)))).

Let's break down the exact tensor flow: ($W_{data}$): It carries the raw facts: "Atlanta Hospital has 5 patients." ($W_{gate}$): It carries the context: "Is it Christmas? Are we legally shut down?" The Smart Valve ($\text{SiLU}$) If it sees a normal Tuesday, it opens the valve wide: 1.0 (100%).If it sees a Christmas holiday, it cranks the valve almost completely shut: 0.00 (0%).

Collision ($\odot$) 5 patients $\times$ Valve (1.0) = 5 patients flow through. 5 patients $\times$ Valve (0.00) = The flow is choked.

Only 0.00 makes it through. Others are clearly understandable.

Now, I will do nn.init.zeros_(self.fc2.weight) Meaning of nn.init_zeros_(self.fc2.weight) : It’s like saying, “Listen PyTorch, I know you just filled fc2 with random numbers, but I am forcefully Overriding you. Erase them all and set them to Exactly Zero(0).” But Why did we do it ? Think, fc1_gate is a team of 256 Detectives. You have to give them random starting coordinates (Random-Init) so they spread out and investigate different parts of the crime scene. fc2 is the Chief Detective. He sits at the end of the Hall. On Day 1, he starts with absolutely zero assumptions (fc2 = 0). He just listens to the 256 diverse theories coming from the detectives, and he slowly starts adjusting his own weights based on which detectives are making the most sense. What is hidden? dim is your standard factory pipe size (e.g., 256). hidden is the internal "thinking space" inside the block. We usually make it wider than dim so the network has room to find complex patterns (e.g., 512). What is encoder_in ? self.encoder_in = nn.Linear(num_past_features, dim) => nn.Linear(What You Have, What The Machine Needs) . Assume We have num_past_features (eg. 15). But The machine needs dim (eg. 256). => encoder_in stretches the 15 real-world facts into a 256-wide tensor so it safely fits into the assembly line. => encoder_in just resizes the data so it fits the machine. What is an encoder ? self.encoder = nn.ModuleList([ResidualBlock(dim) for _ in range(enc_layers)]) If enc_layers = 3, this code creates a list of 3 distinct, independent SwiGLU blocks: [Block 1, Block 2, Block 3]. The loop builds the 3 machines.

nn.ModuleList plugs them into the GPU.

Meaning : ctx = x.mean(dim = 1) + self.static_proj(static_features) x.mean(dim = 1) => Crush all the past history into a single summary Vector.

self.static_proj(static_features) => Encode the unchanging DNA. future_covariates => The Known Future. Facts you already know about the next 36 months before the model even makes a prediction.

prob_active => The Life Switch. (Sigmoid forces 0.0 to 1.0). Answers: "Is this project still alive?" expected_volume => The Effort Engine. (Softplus forces positive numbers). Answers: "If alive, how many hours?" The Merge (prob_active * expected_volume) => The Sudden Death Multiplier.

The Full Code :

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import pytorch_lightning as pl


# HARDWARE Requirement. 

def round_to_multiple(x: int, multiple: int = 64) -> int:
    return ((x + multiple - 1) // multiple) * multiple


class ResidualBlock(nn.Module):
   
    def __init__(self, dim: int, expansion_factor: float = 4.0, dropout: float = 0.0):
        super().__init__()
        
        # Calculate optimal width and align for Tensor Cores
        hidden = int(dim * expansion_factor * (2.0 / 3.0))
        hidden = round_to_multiple(hidden, 64)

        self.fc1_gate = nn.Linear(dim, 2 * hidden, bias=False)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hidden, dim, bias=False)

        # Zero-Init Strategy: Block starts as a perfect identity pass-through
        nn.init.zeros_(self.fc2.weight)

        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout) if dropout > 0 else nn.Identity()
        
        # Native PyTorch 2.1+ C++ Fused RMSNorm (Fastest possible normalization)
        self.norm = nn.RMSNorm(dim)

    def forward(self, x):
        residual = x
        x_proj = self.fc1_gate(x)
        
        # Split into Data Stream and Gate Stream
        x_data, x_gate = x_proj.chunk(2, dim=-1)
        
        # SwiGLU Valve: The gate dictates how much data passes
        h = x_data * F.silu(x_gate)
        
        y = self.dropout(self.fc2(h))
        return self.norm(residual + y)


class ProductionTiDEAdvanced(nn.Module):
   
    def __init__(
        self,):
        super().__init__()
        self.horizon = horizon
        self.dim = dim
        self.out_dim = out_dim

        # Past Data Encoder
        self.encoder_in = nn.Linear(num_past_features, dim)
        self.encoder = nn.ModuleList([AdvancedResidualBlock(dim) for _ in range(enc_layers)])

        # Projections & FiLM Mechanism
        self.static_proj = nn.Linear(num_static_features, dim)
        self.future_proj = nn.Linear(num_future_features, dim)
        self.film = nn.Linear(dim, 2 * dim)

        # Decoder
        self.decoder = nn.ModuleList([AdvancedResidualBlock(dim) for _ in range(dec_layers)])

        # BUSINESS LOGIC: Dual-Head Architecture
        # Probability of project remaining active
        self.activity_head = nn.Linear(dim, out_dim)  
        # Expected volume if active
        self.volume_head = nn.Linear(dim, out_dim)    

    def forward(self, past_input, future_covariates, static_features):
        # Encode Past
        x = self.encoder_in(past_input)
        for blk in self.encoder:
            x = blk(x)

        # Build Context (Time Pool + Static Properties)
        ctx = x.mean(dim=1) + self.static_proj(static_features)

        # Modulate Future (FiLM)
        fut = self.future_proj(future_covariates)
        gamma, beta = self.film(ctx).chunk(2, dim=-1)
        
        # Expand across Time dimension
        gamma = gamma.unsqueeze(1)
        beta  = beta.unsqueeze(1)
        dec   = fut * (1.0 + gamma) + beta

        # Decode 
        for blk in self.decoder:
            dec = blk(dec)

        # Dual-Head Architecture
        prob_active = torch.sigmoid(self.activity_head(dec))
        expected_volume = F.softplus(self.volume_head(dec))
        
        return prob_active * expected_volume

Q: How can I create a set-like array in bash? A:

Use associative arrays:

declare -A dirs

for f in "${filelist[@]}"; do
    dir=$(exec dirname "$f") ## Or dir=${f%/*}
    dirs[$dir]=$dir
done

printf '%s\n' "${dirs[@]}"

Or if input is from file:

readarray -t files < filelist
for f in "${files[@]}"; do
    dir=$(exec dirname "$f") ## Or dir=${f%/*}
    dirs[$dir]=$dir
done
  • Let's keep unnecessary forks on a subshell minimum with exec.

Q: Python socket errno 32 broken pipe A:

maybe SIGPIPE error :

Your server process has received a SIGPIPE writing to a socket. This usually happens when you write to a socket fully closed on the other (client) side. This might be happening when a client program doesn't wait till all the data from the server is received and simply closes a socket (using close function).

In a C program you would normally try setting to ignore SIGPIPE signal or setting a dummy signal handler for it. In this case a simple error will be returned when writing to a closed socket. In your case a python seems to throw an exception that can be handled as a premature disconnect of the client.

Q: Check file type in Linux A:

Linux has a built-in file command: man file

The main difference between Windows and *nix is that DOS/Windows has built-in dependencies on file suffix. For example, an executable must be named ".exe" (or .com); a .bat file must be named ".bat" (or .cmd).

Linux, MacOS, BSD, etc have no such restriction. Instead, they must have "execute" permission set in order to be "runable". This is true for either a binary executable (e.g. compiled code) or a script (e.g. Python, Perl ... or a shell script).

Instead of relying only on file suffix, the "file" command also looks at self-identifying "magic numbers" or other "header information" in the file itself.

SUGGESTION:

If the built-in "file" doesn't meet your needs; perhaps you can wrap it in a shell script that:

1) Checks for certain "well known suffixes" (use basename to extract the suffix), and/or

2) Calls "file" as a fallback
